title: Bright Yellow 'Golden Tree' Coral Is So Strange It Needed a New Family
summary:
Deep in the Pacific Ocean off Costa Rica, scientists have found a bright yellow coral so unusual that it does not fit into any known coral family. To classify it, they had to create a brand-new family.

The coral grows in branching shapes that look like trees. Some colonies are more than a meter tall, which is over 3 feet. It was found between 360 and 529 meters below the surface, on underwater mountains called seamounts. Researchers used a remotely operated underwater robot named SuBastian to collect samples during expeditions in 2019 and 2023.

The coral grew on rocky spots where brittle stars, relatives of starfish, covered almost every surface. The yellow branches seemed to rise from the seafloor like glowing trees surrounded by stars.

That scene inspired its name. The scientists used Quenya, the Elvish language invented by J.R.R. Tolkien, author of "The Lord of the Rings." The group name Laurinque means "golden tree," and the species name elenya means "of the stars."

Figuring out where the coral belonged was tricky. Scientists first checked three genes often used to sort corals, but each gene pointed to a different family. So they compared hundreds of genes at once. That showed the coral is a separate branch on the family tree, most closely related to a family called Eunicellidae but different enough to get its own family, Laurinqueidae.

Lead researcher Odalisca Breedy of the University of Costa Rica said she was amazed by the beauty of the coral garden when she first saw it.

The discovery shows how much of the deep ocean is still unexplored. Coral gardens like this give homes to many other deep-sea creatures. The study was published in the journal ZooKeys.
why_it_matters: The find shows how much of the deep ocean remains unknown and why coral gardens, which give homes to many deep-sea creatures, are worth studying and protecting.

background_read: Corals are animals made of many tiny creatures living together, and some grow in the deep, dark ocean far from sunlight.
Scientists sort living things into groups such as species, genus and family based on how closely related they are.
Comparing genes lets scientists see which living things share common ancestors, which helps them place a new find on the family tree.
Much of the deep ocean has never been explored, so researchers use underwater robots to study and collect creatures there.
